title: The Notebook and the Tapes
standfirst: Nine days of one war, held in two minds that cannot reach each other.

epigraph.rendering: When a man does you wrong, consider at once what conception of good or evil he had when he did it. For when you see that, you will pity him, and not be surprised or angry.

left.label: The Notebook
left.note: Kept in his daughter's green school exercise book, returned in her bag.

right.label: The Tapes
right.byline: The President, dictated for an authorized memoir
right.note: Transcribed by a ghostwriter who is present but never recorded.

notebook: They gave me back her bag on Sunday. It was in a pile with forty others behind the mosque on Farjam Street and a young man with a clipboard was writing names on masking tape. He asked me twice how to spell Rahmani. He was maybe nineteen. His hands were shaking worse than mine.
The bag is pink with a cartoon fox on it. The strap is torn but the buckle still works. Inside there was a water bottle, still half full, and a pencil case, and this notebook.

I am writing in her notebook. On the first eleven pages there is her handwriting. Multiplication tables. A drawing of our neighbor's cat with the ears too big. On page four she has written her full name eight times in a row, practicing, each one a little neater than the last, because she was proud that her name was long.
Yasaman.

I do not know what else to say. Roya has not spoken since Tuesday. She sits in the kitchen with the light off. My mother came from Karaj and cooked for two days and then went home because there was no one to feed.
Milad has not cried. He is fifteen. He watches the ceiling.

They hit the transformer station and the building beside it, and the school is one hundred and sixty meters from the transformer station. I have measured it on the map with my thumb. One hundred and sixty meters. She was nine years old.
tape: Is it on? The light's red. Marisol, red means it's— okay. Okay. What are we— right. The four days. Put this at the front, gold letters if the book can do gold.

Four presidents sat in that chair and sucked their thumbs. Four. And I walk in and in four days, four, I did the thing they couldn't do in— how long, doesn't matter, twenty five years, put twenty five. The thing. You know the thing. She knows the thing.

The footage, though. Have you seen the footage. It's a movie. Better than a movie. I told Danny, score it, get real music, the big music, because nobody feels a thing until you tell them to feel it, that's television, and the presidency is a television show, the biggest one ever made, and I am the biggest star it has ever had. Bigger than the actors. I'd have been the greatest actor who ever lived if I'd wanted it, everybody says so, but I chose this instead.

Now. They're going to show you a school. There'll be a little pink bag, a shoe, they have the shoe ready before the smoke clears, and I want this in bold and I want it once: that was not us. That was not an American weapon. Ours are beautiful, ours are surgical, I have held the drawings, and whatever hit that building was theirs or it was made in a computer. Half of what they run is made in a computer now and the other half they do to their own people to get on the news. Do not believe your eyes. Your eyes are the stupidest part of you. Ask any magician. I know all of them. They love me.

And even if— which it was not— but even if, they built the school around the thing on purpose, so that when nothing happens they get to stand there and say something happened. It is very sophisticated. It is also nothing. It is sophisticated nothing.

The decision itself, the big one, nobody in that room would say it out loud, sixty year old men with the résumés and not one finishes a sentence, so I finished it for them. Clean, I said. And it was clean. The most precise weapons ever built and we built them, I built them, after they let everything rot.

What was I— Marisol, what's the day. Doesn't matter. Historic day. I'm tired, four days no sleep and I'm sharper than all of them are at nine in the morning, put that, and take out the knee, I never said the knee, the knee is perfect.

canon.rendering: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the judgments they form about things.
canon.note: The two men receive the same four days. One receives them as the largest decision made in that room in fifty years. One receives them as a torn pink strap and a bottle still half full. Nothing in the events settles which reading is correct, because the events are not doing the work; the assent is. And notice already where his assent will not go. Told a school was hit, he does not argue that it fails to matter, he argues that it did not happen, that the weapon was not his, that the eyes reporting it cannot be trusted. This is not yet a lie. It is the first refusal of the one impression the next five months will keep setting in front of him and that he will never once accept: that the hand was his.

notebook: Tomorrow is the New Year and the year is going to turn whether I permit it or not. This is the part nobody warns you about. The world does not pause for you. The equinox arrives on schedule.

Roya set the sofreh anyway. I came home and there it was on the floor of the living room, the cloth, the mirror, the wheat sprouting in its dish because she planted it two weeks ago out of a habit older than her grief. She put out the goldfish. She put out the coins and the garlic and the vinegar. Then she sat back on her heels and looked at it for a long time and said, very quietly, that she had bought seven of everything before, and now there was one of us missing and the number seven still worked, and she could not explain why that felt like an insult.

Two nights ago was Chaharshanbe Suri. In our street some boys lit a fire in a barrel and jumped it, the way I did when I was their age, the way I did with her last year holding both her hands so she could clear it. Zardi-ye man az to, sorkhi-ye to az man. My yellow to you, your red to me. Give me your health and take my sickness.

I could hear the anti aircraft over Ekbatan while they were jumping. Someone shouted at them to put it out because of the aircraft, and someone else shouted back that the whole sky was already lit, so what did one barrel matter.
He was right. But they put it out anyway.
tape: The strait. Okay. The strait.
NOBODY. TOLD ME. THEY COULD DO THAT.

Capital letters, all of it, I don't care how it looks on the page, because they will rewrite this later and I want it fresh, in my voice, angry, the way it actually was. I sat in that room in the winter and I said, what about the strait. One question. Off the top of my head. No briefing book, I don't read the briefing books, reading is for people who cannot think, I have the instinct and the instinct has never once been wrong. And a man with a doctorate told me: weeks to close, days to reopen.
Eleven hours. ELEVEN HOURS.

Explain to me how a man from Queens with no degree is the only person in a building full of doctorates who thought of the ocean. I'll tell you how. They don't think. They retrieve. They go pull the old memo and change the date on the top and hand it back to you like it's thinking.

So now there's a number on every gas sign in America and they'll call it my number, it's never their number, always mine, and the same people who begged me to do it— and they begged, I have the room, I remember the room, I think I remember the room— are on the television now with the long faces about gas.

And their guy sits across from me and reads me a list. A list! I'm looking at satellite, their whole air defense is a parking lot, gone, and he reads me demands off a piece of paper like he won. Marty says it's cultural, they open impossible, it's a bazaar thing, they haggle. Fine. But somebody has to be the adult, and it will not be me, because I'm the one holding everything and also I get to be the child, I get to be both, that is the fun of the whole thing, nobody understands that about me.
What else. Somebody put the knee out there. That came from inside. Nine people knew. Write it down: find the nine.

canon.rendering: To blame others for your own troubles is the mark of a beginner. To blame yourself is the mark of one who has started. To blame no one is the mark of one whose schooling is finished.
canon.note: Three sentences into the second session he reaches for the first rung and stays there for the remaining eight months. Notice that he is not lying: someone did give him a bad estimate on the strait, and the claim is true. That is exactly what makes it fatal to his education. A true grievance with an author who is not him lets the whole failure be filed under another name, and once it is filed there is nothing left in it to examine. The father is on the same ladder facing the other way, and by the fourth entry he is furious at his own government as well — not wisdom yet, but the second rung, which is the one the president never reaches: the place where the buck arrives at your own desk and stops.

notebook: Forty days.

We went to Behesht e Zahra this morning. There is a section now that did not exist in February and it is not full, which is the thing I cannot stop thinking about. There is room. Somebody has planned for room.

My brother called from Vancouver again. Third time this month. He wants us to try for Turkey, he says he has a friend, he says there are still ways. He talks fast, the way people talk when they are ashamed of where they are standing. I told him the airports are closed and the roads east are checkpoints and Roya will not leave the country that has Yasaman in the ground in it. He said, Bijan, she is not in the ground, she is with God. I said that is very easy to say from a place where nothing falls out of the sky.
Then I hung up and sat in the car in the parking lot of the cemetery for twenty minutes and I was so ashamed of myself I could not go back in to my wife.
I want to write down what I actually feel, since no one asks me and no one will.

I do not think the men who did this know that our street exists. That is the part. If they hated me it would be simpler. Hate is a relationship. This is not a relationship. Some person read a grid reference off a screen and my daughter was inside the rounding error. They will say the transformer station was a legitimate military target and maybe by their books it was, I am not a lawyer, I fix water mains.

But I would like to say this to whoever it was, quite calmly. She was learning multiplication. She could do the sevens but not the eights. Her name was long and she was proud of it. You did not kill an argument about a nuclear program. You killed a person who was working on her eights.
tape: Dover. I want to do Dover. Is the machine— it's going. Good.

You stand there and they bring them off the plane, the boxes, the flags, and there's a family and they look at you. Right at you. And I did it, I stood the whole time, I did not check my watch, some of them check the watch, I have watched them check the watch, animals. I performed it perfectly. Career people came to me afterward, hard men, and said that was the finest they had ever seen it done, better than the movies, and one of them cried, and I comforted him, I comforted the one who was supposed to comfort me. Put that in. That is the kind of man I am.
A woman said something to me on the tarmac and I said something back, beautiful, and I won't repeat it because it was private and also I don't— it's private.
They'll write forty stories about a school we did not touch and zero about me in the cold at six in the morning being magnificent about grief. Nobody writes the magnificent part.

Who had my schedule. Three outlets had Dover before we announced it. Nine people knew. It is always the nine. I've asked for the list twice, Danny says leave it, and I said Danny, everything is the list, there is nothing in this life that is not the list.

How long has it been. Six weeks? You cannot judge a thing at six weeks, only a fool or a liar judges at six weeks and most of them are both. The program is finished. Finished forever. A hundred years after everyone in this room is dust I'll be on the money and the ones crying on the television will be on nothing.

canon.rendering: When you see a man weeping in grief, do not be carried off by the appearance. Say first that it is not the loss that afflicts him, since another bears the same loss lightly, but the judgment he has made about it. Do not refuse to console him with words, and even to grieve with him outwardly. But take care that you do not also grieve inwardly.
canon.note: Epictetus describes a hard discipline: full outward presence, no inward collapse. At Dover the president performs the outward half so completely that he comforts the man who came to comfort him and reports it was done better than the movies. The inward half never occurs, because the inward half would require him to stand in front of the coffins as the reason they are there. He grades the performance instead. Read against the tarmac the passage stops being permission for coldness and becomes a diagnostic, and it is worth asking which half you would fail.

notebook: The blockade is two weeks old and the city has started to change shape.

At work we are down to one shift because the pumping station at Kan has been running on the diesel generator since the grid attacks and there is no diesel to spare, so we rotate the pressure by district. This is my job now. Deciding which neighborhoods get water in the morning and which get it at night. Yesterday a woman on Delavaran screamed at me in the street for eleven minutes because her mother is on dialysis and the tank on the roof was empty. I stood there and let her. She was correct. There was nothing to say back to her.

Prices. I write them down because in a year I will not believe them. Chicken has tripled since February. Cooking oil you buy from a man, not a shop. The pharmacy on the corner has a handwritten list taped inside the glass of what they do not have, and the list is longer than the shelves. Insulin is on the list. My aunt's chemotherapy is on the list. They tell us on the radio that medicine is exempt from the blockade, and technically this is true, and technically it does not matter, because no shipping company on earth will send a hull into that water for the sake of a container of ampoules.
So the exemption is real and the medicine is not real. I have thought about this a lot while sitting in traffic. It is a very modern kind of cruelty. Nobody has to sign anything.

And here is the other half, and I will write it even though I would burn this notebook before letting anyone read it. There are men in this city whose families flew out in the first week. Everybody knows which ones. We have been told for twenty years to endure for the sake of resistance and I have endured, I have endured the sanctions and the inflation and the shutdowns and the humiliation of watching my salary become a joke, and I would endure more, but not for them. Not for the ones who evacuated their children.
I am being crushed between two things and only one of them is dropping bombs. That does not make the other one my friend.
tape: Business side today. The book needs the business side, that's what people buy, the publisher won't say it but she knows.

While all of this is going on I'm also doing the biggest deals in the history of the region. The fund. The largest pile of money ever assembled by anyone, and they came to me, the direction matters, they came to me, because there is one man over there they trust and it is not the State Department. The State Department has been wrong about that part of the world for sixty straight years. Sixty! You could flip a coin. You could ask a horse.

Is the family involved, they'll ask. Everything's lawyered, the best lawyers, separate entity, and if my family can't do business then no president's family could and that's not America. My kids are talented. More talented than me in some ways. Not most ways.

The tower is not a conflict. Somebody wrote the tower's a conflict. The tower is a BUILDING. The most beautiful building in the region, the tallest, with my name across the top of it in gold, and you can see it from the water in the evening, and a man should be able to stand at the water and see his own name burning up there against the dark. That is not corruption. That is the reward for winning. They just cannot stand for me to have one beautiful thing.
Now. Hollis. General Hollis comes to me Friday with the whole speech. The off ramp, sir. The stockpiles, sir. And I let him talk, I always let a man finish, it saves me the trouble of the rope.

There is one in every organization. Always very handsome. Great posture, the documentary voice, and what he wants underneath all of it is for nothing to ever happen, because nothing happening is the one thing that can never be pinned on him. That is not courage. Everybody calls it courage now. That is a pension with a haircut.

And then forty eight hours later his exact words, off ramp, two words, are in the paper. So he leaked it or he told the leaker, there is no third door, Marisol, don't look at me, there is no third door in that room. He is not warning me. He is building the alibi. Write it down. Write it twice. Hollis is building the alibi.

canon.rendering: Wherever a man places his I and his mine, there he must incline.
canon.note: One doctrine demonstrated twice. He has placed his I in the fund, the tower, the name burning in gold over the water, the appearance of strength, so his judgment inclines there with no felt sensation of bending. And because he assumes every man is built the same way, he can read General Hollis only one way: a man protecting a pension. He is not being cynical. He is being consistent. He has no available theory of a person who has placed his I somewhere else — which is also why the strike can never be his. He has staked the whole self on being the winner of it, and the winner of a thing is not the one it indicts.

notebook: They called it a ceasefire for nine days and then last night the sky opened again over the south of the city and once over Tehran, and this morning the word ceasefire is just a sound people make.
Nothing else to report. Milad asked me at breakfast what the word means if it can be turned off. I did not have an answer so I told him to eat.
tape: Short one. Not in the mood. The head's— it's fine, it's a long day.
They hit our ships, we hit back, that's the whole story, and I won't apologize for it during a ceasefire or a Tuesday or anything else. You break it, you own it.

And I barely— write this down. That was Coyle's package, end of a nineteen hour day, they slid it across the table, and I said if it's clean, go. Four words. If it's clean, go. I didn't read the pages. You don't read the pages, that's what the people are for, I read the man's face and the face was clean.

Now. Ask Danny, quietly, not in an email, whether the second wave was in the thing I approved or whether it got added after. Because I have gone over it in my head, I don't know, forty times, and I remember one wave. One. And if somebody put a second wave under my four words, that is a very serious— ask him with your mouth, not in writing.
What was the— Marisol, who did we hit today. Doesn't matter. Take that out. Take out who did we hit. Leave the four words.

canon.rendering: Every error contains a contradiction. The one who errs does not wish to err, but has been forced by what appeared true to him.
canon.note: The shortest entries in both documents sit on the doctrinal center of the page. He said if it is clean, go — four words of assent at the end of a long day, given, he now admits, without reading the pages, and followed by a note to find out afterward whether the second wave was even in the thing he approved. Socratic intellectualism is not the claim that he meant well. It is the harder claim that the moment of assent is the whole moral event, and that a mind trained to skip it — to sign without reading, to approve a face instead of a page — will produce an atrocity while experiencing itself as barely present at the scene. That is how the buck never reaches him. He was never, by his own account, quite there when it was passed.

notebook: There is a document now. A memorandum. They are calling it a path to ending the war and it was signed by people I could not pick out of a photograph, and for four days this house has been infected with hope, which I did not expect and did not want.
Hope is dangerous in the way that standing up too fast is dangerous. You forget you have been on the floor.

Roya went to the bazaar on Tuesday for the first time since March. She came back with fabric. She is going to make curtains for the back room. She has not made anything since Yasaman, and she stood in the doorway with the bag in her hand and looked at me almost defiantly, as if daring me to say it was too soon, and I said the color was good. It is a kind of green. It is not a color I would have picked. It is the best thing that has happened in this house in four months.
I went back to full days at the department. There is talk of restoring the eastern line. I caught myself planning something for October and had to sit down.

Here is what I have understood about the shape of this. I used to think grief was a weight you carry and slowly put down. It is not. It is a room you live in, and some days the door is open and you walk out into the street and you are a man buying bread, and then you turn around and you are back inside it and you were never anywhere else. Yasaman is in every room in this house. I do not want that fixed. If someone offered me a medicine that made me stop feeling this I would refuse it, because the feeling is the last place she is still doing anything.
tape: So we have peace. Somebody— we have peace. There's a document.

The prize thing first, because they'll ask. I don't care about it, everyone knows I don't care, they gave it to a man once for a SPEECH, a speech, and I ended a war, but I don't care, put that I don't care, and put it in twice so they understand how much I don't care.

Did I read it. The document. No. Of course not. It's forty pages, I'm told forty, could be four hundred, and reading it is not the job. They hand you the pen and they show you the line and the line is the job. Marty read it, or somebody read it, one of them read it, and they said sign, and a signature from me is worth more than forty pages from anybody alive, so if you think about it I brought the value and they brought the paper.

What's in it. I'll find out. What's in it is peace, that's what's in it, the rest is lawyers making themselves necessary. And if it's wrong we do it again, that's the beauty, nothing is ever actually finished, that's the secret they don't tell you, you can always, always do it again.

Marty called at four in the morning, which he never does, and said sir, they signed. And I want the moment described, big, because you cannot get it from the coverage. I stood up. I put on the robe, the good one, and I walked the colonnade in the dark, alone, and I said out loud, to nobody: they will build rooms about this. Rooms. With my voice playing in them. Children on buses. And I meant it and I want it in the book exactly like that.

A hundred and thirteen days. Every person who said I would blunder into a forever war is now looking at a signed piece of paper that I did not read and did not need to read. That is leadership. Leadership is being right without doing the reading.
Okay, enough, I'm getting— it's late, and I am not a sentimental man, do not write sentimental. Actually, write that I got a little sentimental, it plays well, it's good for the book. But I didn't.

canon.rendering: One man, when he has done a service, is ready to enter it in the account as a favor owed. Another is not ready to do that, but in his own mind he thinks of the man as in his debt. A third, in a way, does not even know what he has done. He is like a vine that has produced grapes and asks nothing more once it has borne its fruit.
canon.note: Marcus praises the man who does good the way a vine bears grapes: without noticing, asking nothing further once the fruit is on the branch. Read the passage against a man who signs a peace he did not read and whose first movement is to put on the robe, walk the colonnade, and picture the rooms that will be built around the sound of his own voice. In the same days the father comes home to a green fabric he would not have chosen and calls it the best thing to happen in his house in four months, and it does not occur to him to be seen doing it. That is the vine. The tape is the exact opposite of the vine: fruit he never grew, held up to a camera before he has bothered to ask what it is.

notebook: It is over. The memorandum, I mean. Two days ago the American president said the truce was finished and now the ships are burning again in the strait and last night the phones lost signal for six hours.
I want to record what happened in this house on Tuesday because I am afraid of it.

Milad came home and told me, in the doorway, with his shoes still on, that he had been to speak to someone about volunteering. He is fifteen. He said it the way boys say things they have rehearsed in their heads on the walk home. He said he cannot sit in a room and do nothing while they do this to us. He said Yasaman's name to me, which he has not done since March, and he used it like a stone.
I hit him. I have never hit either of my children. I hit my son across the face in the hallway of my own home and Roya came out of the kitchen and the three of us stood there.
Then I put my arms around him and I said, I have one child left, and I do not care about anything else in the world, and he cried finally, four months late, standing up, into my shoulder.
I do not know if I have stopped him or delayed him.

Let me be honest here, since this book is the only place I am honest. I understand him. There is a thing in my chest that wants what he wants. When I read that they hit a fuel depot and killed nobody I am disappointed, and I have to sit with the fact that I am the kind of man who is disappointed by that now. In February I was not that man. This is what they have done, and I do not think they have the faintest idea they are doing it. They think they are destroying centrifuges. They are manufacturing fifteen year olds.
tape: THEY PLAYED ME.
I want played in the book. In the chapter title. Chapter— what number are we on. Doesn't matter. Chapter Played. Let them run that.

They signed the thing— the thing I didn't need to read, and they were right, look what it was worth— they signed it with zero intention, ZERO, of honoring one line, and they used the days to move their assets back into the water, and now there are people in this town getting ready to write that I was naive. Naive! At my age! After ninety three years of these people— however many years, a lot of years, more than anyone living— I'm the naive one. I gave them one chance. Any decent man gives one chance and they showed the whole world what they are.

So the truce is finished. I said it and I meant it and this time there is no version where I stop early. None. And I want it clear, for the book: I am not an angry man. I'm the calmest one in any room, ask Hollis— don't ask Hollis— ask anyone. But there is a difference between being angry and knowing exactly who did what to you, and I know exactly, and the entire history of the world is people finding out too late what happens next.

They knew, by the way. Somebody told them. You do not sign on a Thursday and reposition on a Friday unless you already know what we will do about it. Somebody in this building is handing them my limits. Explain the timing to me. Explain the timing and I'll drop it. Nobody can explain the timing.

They think I'll get bored. That's the whole strategy. Three of my own people tell me that's the read over there, the American gets bored, loses interest, wanders off. Eighty years old and the plan of a nation of ninety million people is that I'll wander off. Marisol, stop writing— now write this— we'll see who wanders off. We'll see who's still standing in the ashes. Burn the— we'll see.

canon.rendering: Anger is an appetite for repaying pain, and there is no swifter road to madness. See what wreckage it makes of cities and of households.
canon.note: Two men are injured within days of each other and both convert the injury into a program. The president wants the word played in a chapter title and, by the end of the session, is reaching for fire. Milad, at fifteen, goes to speak to someone about volunteering. Seneca's point is not that anger is unpleasant but that it is a form of belief: it carries the judgment that harm has been done to you and that repayment is owed to you. Both judgments arrive feeling like perception rather than opinion — which is why, across eight months of tape, harm is always something done to him and never once something done by him. The only person in either document who interrupts the sequence has to do it with his hands, in a hallway, and is ashamed.

notebook: I am going to write carefully now and then I am going to move this notebook.

They took Reza's nephew on Thursday. Twenty three years old, works at a phone repair kiosk on Resalat, and the charge is contact with a hostile service. Reza says the boy sold a used handset to someone. That is what Reza says. I do not know what is true. What I know is the number, because the number gets out even now: hundreds this year, dozens last month alone, and every week the rope and the announcement afterward.

So this is the country in August. Above us the aircraft. Around us the men who are so frightened of us that they have started killing us at a pace they did not manage in peacetime. The bombing gave them the thing they always wanted, which is an emergency, and inside an emergency there is no such thing as an innocent question.

Nobody outside will hold both of these in their head at once. To the Americans I am a regime. To the regime I am a suspect. There is no room anywhere in the world for me to stand and be simply a man from Tehranpars whose daughter died and who would like the water pressure restored in district nine.

I heard a number on a foreign broadcast last week. One hundred and sixty eight children. I know that number is a claim, and I know somebody in an office somewhere is preparing a document arguing that the real figure is lower, and they may even be right. Yasaman is somewhere inside that number. She has become a data point in a dispute between two governments about whose arithmetic is more honest. That is what has happened to my daughter. She was a person who liked the cat with the big ears and now she is evidence.
I am putting this book behind the water heater tonight.
tape: Four in the morning. Can't sleep. Just talk, fix it later.

There's a report going around, civilian numbers, somebody handed it to the Hill and it's out, and I want two things down. One: the report says we were careful, which we were, the most careful military in the history of the world, more careful than careful. Two: whoever leaked it is a traitor, and I've said it out loud and I'll say it here.

And the numbers are invented anyway. You understand that. There is an office somewhere whose entire job is to make up a number and then cry about it. A hundred and sixty eight children. A hundred and sixty eight. Where do you get a number like that? You get it from a man who was paid to write it down. Half those children were never born. Do not believe the number, and do not believe the little pictures either, the pictures are the easiest thing in the world to make now, a child can make one on a telephone, and the enemy has whole buildings of people who do nothing but make the pictures.

And nobody says the other thing. They are hanging their own. Four hundred and forty four this year, kids from phone shops, in a yard, and where is the outrage, WHERE, not one of the organizations that has a feeling about me every eleven minutes has said a single word.

I keep— this is off the record. Danny's people flagged a picture. A girl. From the first days. And I looked at it, and I want to be very clear, that is not a real— I don't know that that is real, and even if it is real I had nothing to do with it, we did not hit that building, the people who put a weapon next to a school did that, the four presidents did that, her own government did that, they had every chance and they spent it. But I looked at it. I looked at it for a while and then I put it face down on the desk.

Marisol. Is this on. It's on. Take out from the picture. From 'Danny's people' to here, take it out. Leave the four hundred and forty four. And I want the file, not a copy, the file, and if there is a backup I want to know where the backup lives, because I have been doing this eighty years and there is always, always a backup.

canon.rendering: Make for yourself a definition of the thing presented: see it stripped, whole, and divided into what it is made of, and name it, and name the parts it will be resolved into.
canon.note: The central Stoic discipline is to look at the impression until you can say what it actually is. Both men refuse the same exercise on the same night, in opposite directions. He is handed the photograph and will not let it be a photograph: the number is invented, the pictures are manufactured, and even while he looks at it he is saying it is not real — and then, because some part of him has seen it anyway, he asks for the file, not a copy, the file. The father hides his notebook behind the water heater for the reverse reason: he has looked too clearly to be safe writing it down. One is kept from the impression by fear. The other has power enough to order the impression destroyed rather than name it — the last desk the buck could have stopped at, and the one he burns.

notebook: Quiet week. Two nights with nothing overhead. You learn to hear the quiet as a held breath rather than as peace, but I will take it.

The pomegranate in the yard has set fruit. It is a bad tree, it has always been a bad tree, my father in law planted it in the wrong corner in 1994 and it gets four hours of sun and produces maybe nine fruit in a good year. Yasaman was the one who cared about it. She used to count them in July and report the number to me at dinner like a foreman.
There are eleven this year. Eleven. The best it has ever done.
I stood out there yesterday evening for a long time, longer than I meant to, and I want to write down what I thought, because it was not what I expected to think.

I thought: I am not going to get justice. There will be no moment. No one is coming to this house to say her name and mean it. There will be a settlement or an exhaustion or a new government or a slow forgetting, and in ten years this will be a chapter with a name in somebody's book, and I will be a man in his fifties with a bad back and one son.

And under that I thought: I will not become the thing that did this. That is the only piece of it I control. I have almost no power in my life now. I cannot protect my family, I cannot leave, I cannot vote for anything that matters, I cannot even guarantee water on the fourth floor of a building on Delavaran on a Tuesday. But I can decide what I turn into. Milad watches me. He will take his shape from what he sees me do, and if what he sees is a man who kept working, who did not hand himself over to the hatred, who counted pomegranates, then something survives that they cannot reach with any munition they have.

That is not forgiveness. I want to be extremely clear about that, in case anyone ever reads this. I do not forgive them. I do not forgive the ones who ordered it or the ones who justified it afterward or the comfortable people who watched it on a screen and thought about something else within the hour. I hope they are made to look at what they did, in detail, by name, one child at a time.
But I am not going to spend what is left of my life inside that. She would not have known me.
Roya finished the curtains. They are up. The green is still not a color I would have picked.
tape: Good week. Quiet week. Oman's calling. Oman always calls, they call from Oman the way other people breathe.

I've decided on the thing on the water. Not a museum, museums are for dead men. A working institute, mine, and we rebuild the room, the actual table, and the screens show what I was seeing that night, and you stand where I stood, and my voice is in it, my voice in every room telling you what it was. And a theater. A real theater in the middle of the whole thing, because at the center of a monument like this there should be a stage, and on certain nights— we'll see. We'll see what happens on the stage.

Kids come through on the buses. That's the part I love. Some kid from nowhere walks in and sees what it actually takes, because everyone has an opinion about the decision and about eleven human beings in all of history have ever had to make one.

Was it worth it. They'll ask it in every interview until I die and I want the answer in the book so I never have to say it again: you don't get to ask that yet. You ask that in fifty years. Nobody asked Truman at year one. They were killing Lincoln in the papers in year two, and now he's on the money and the men who wrote those columns are on nothing.
History is not written by people crying on television. It gets written later, by serious people, with the whole picture. That's the last line. Use that.

And Marisol. Before you go. The session from the second, the late one, the picture. Did you take it out or is it still sitting somewhere. Take it out. And the transcript, and whatever's on the card, and the backup, I want the backup, everybody has a— just take it out. What were we— it's late. Take it out.

canon.rendering: Some things are up to us and some are not. Up to us are judgment, impulse, desire, aversion, and in a word whatever is our own doing. Not up to us are the body, property, reputation, office, and in a word whatever is not our own doing.
canon.note: The father arrives at the division without the vocabulary. He lists everything he cannot do, which is nearly all of it, and then says that what he turns into is the only piece he controls, and that his son will take his shape from it. That is prohairesis stated by a water engineer in a yard. The president spends his final session on the institute, the recreated room, the stage at its center, his voice in every gallery — which is to say he stakes the whole account on reputation, the one thing wholly outside him. He even reaches for Truman, whose desk carried the sign that the buck stops here, and does not hear it: he has spent nine days proving his own desk to be the single place in the world where it never does. He is not less intelligent than the father. He has drawn the line in the only spot where nothing can be secured, and he will spend the rest of his life defending ground that was never his.
